topic.name: The Total Area Bounded by a Single Polar Curve

question.text: Find the total area bounded by the polar curve $r =\cos(3\theta)$ shown above.
question.explanation:
First, we want to find the interval for $\theta$ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or \begin{align*} \cos(3\theta) &= 0. \end{align*}

This gives us two solutions for $3\theta\in[-\pi,\pi)\mathbin{:}$ \[ 3\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{6} \]

So, the first petal is traversed for $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

Since there are $3$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

\begin{align*} A_{\textrm{total}} &= 3 \cdot A_{\textrm{petal}} \\[5pt] & = 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \cos^2(3\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} (1+\cos(6\theta)) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} \left.\left( \theta + \dfrac{1}{6}\sin(6\theta) \right)\right|_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} \left[ \left( \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{1}{6}\sin(\pi) \right) - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{1}{6}\sin(-\pi)\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Total Area Bounded by a Single Polar Curve

question.text: The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{3}\sin(5\theta)$ is given by the integral \[ A = \displaystyle \dfrac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/5} \sin^2(5\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta. \] Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?
question.explanation:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $5$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is \[ A = \dfrac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/5} \sin^2(5\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta. \]

The $1$st petal is traversed from $\theta_1=0$ to $\theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{5},$ and the length of this interval is $\dfrac{\pi}{5}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_3 &= \theta_1+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = 0 + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{5}\\[5pt] \theta_4 &= \theta_2+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{5} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5} \end{align*}

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_5 &= \theta_3+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{5} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5} \\[5pt] \theta_6 &= \theta_4+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{3\pi}{5} \end{align*}

Now, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_7 &= \theta_5+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{3\pi}{5}\\[5pt] \theta_8 &= \theta_6+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{3\pi}{5} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{4\pi}{5} \end{align*}

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fifth petal, we add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the fourth petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_9 &= \theta_7+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{4\pi}{5}\\[5pt] \theta_{10} &= \theta_8+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{4\pi}{5} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = {\pi} \end{align*}

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $5$ petals of our rose: \[ \underbrace{\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$1$st}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{\pi}{5},\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$2$nd}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{5},\dfrac{3\pi}{5} \right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$3$rd}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{3\pi}{5},\dfrac{4\pi}{5} \right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$4$th}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{4\pi}{5},\pi \right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$5$th}} \]

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta = 0$ to $\theta = \pi\mathbin{:}$

\[ A_\textrm{total} = \dfrac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^2(5\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta \]

question.text: Find the total area bounded by the polar curve $r = \sqrt{6}\sin(5\theta),$ shown above.
question.explanation:
First, we want to find the interval for $\theta$ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or

\begin{align*} \sqrt{6}\sin(5\theta) &= 0 \\[5pt] \sin(5\theta) &= 0. \end{align*}

This gives us two solutions for $5\theta \in [0,2\pi]$: \[ 5\theta = 0, \pi \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta= 0, \dfrac{\pi}{5} \]

As a result, the first petal is traversed for $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{5}.$

Since there are $5$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

\begin{align*} A_{\textrm{total}} &= 5 \cdot A_{\textrm{petal}} \\[5pt] &= 5 \cdot 3 \int_{0}^{\pi/5} \sin^2(5\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= 15 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/5} (1-\cos(10\theta)) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left.\left( \theta - \dfrac{1}{10}\sin(10\theta) \right)\right|_{0}^{\pi/5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left[ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{5} - \dfrac{1}{10}\sin(2\pi) \right) - \left(0 - \dfrac{1}{10}\sin(0)\right) \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left( \dfrac{\pi}{5} - 0 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \end{align*}

question.text: The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=2\cos\left(5\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ (shown above) is given by the integral \[ A = \displaystyle 2\int_{-3\pi/20}^{\pi/20} \cos^2\left(5\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta. \] Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?
question.explanation:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $5$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is \[ A = 2\int_{-3\pi/20}^{\pi/20} \cos^2\left(5\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta. \]

The $1$st petal is traversed from $\theta_1=-\dfrac{3\pi}{20}$ to $\theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{20},$ and the length of this interval is $\dfrac{\pi}{5}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_3 &= \theta_1+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = -\dfrac{3\pi}{20} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{20}\\[5pt] \theta_4 &= \theta_2+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{20} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{align*}

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_5 &= \theta_3+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{20} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \\[5pt] \theta_6 &= \theta_4+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{9\pi}{20} \end{align*}

Now, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_7 &= \theta_5+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{9\pi}{20}\\[5pt] \theta_8 &= \theta_6+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{9\pi}{20} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{13\pi}{20} \end{align*}

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fifth petal, we add $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the fourth petal:

\begin{align*} \theta_9 &= \theta_7+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{9\pi}{20} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{13\pi}{20}\\[5pt] \theta_{10} &= \theta_8+ \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{13\pi}{20} + \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{17\pi}{20} \end{align*}

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $5$ petals of our rose: \[ \underbrace{\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{20},\dfrac{\pi}{20}\right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$1$st}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{\pi}{20},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$2$nd}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{9\pi}{20} \right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$3$rd}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{9\pi}{20},\dfrac{13\pi}{20} \right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$4$th}}, \quad \underbrace{\left[\dfrac{13\pi}{20},\dfrac{17\pi}{20} \right]}_{\color{black}\textrm{$5$th}} \]

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta = -\dfrac{3\pi}{10}$ to $\theta = \dfrac{17\pi}{20}\mathbin{:}$

\[ A_\textrm{total} = 2 \int_{-3\pi/20}^{17\pi/20} \cos^2\left(5\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \]

question.text: Find the total area bounded by the polar curve $r =3\cos(2\theta),$ shown above.
question.explanation:
First, we want to find the interval for $\theta$ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or \[ 3\cos(2\theta) = 0. \] This gives us two solutions for $2\theta \in [-\pi,\pi)\mathbin{:}$ \[ 2\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\pi}{4} \]

As a result, the first petal is traversed for $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

Since there are $4$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

\begin{align*} A_{\textrm{total}} &= 4 \cdot A_{\textrm{petal}} \\[5pt] &= 4 \cdot \dfrac{9}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \cos^2(2\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= 18\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} (1+\cos(4\theta)) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &=9 \left.\left( \theta + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(4\theta) \right)\right|_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \\[5pt] &= 9\left[ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(\pi) \right) - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(-\pi)\right) \right] \\[5pt] &=9 \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9\pi}{2} \end{align*}
